title: NEW Lawsuit Against OpenAI Gets at the Heart of the Big Tech Business Model. Schools Might Want to Take Heed.
author: Emily Cherkin
summary: Emily Cherkin describes a lawsuit filed against OpenAI on October 13, 2026 by the EdTech Law Center and co-counsel, alleging that the company takes private information from children without parental consent to train its models. She presents it as a case about consent and about a business model fundamentally at odds with healthy child development, comparing chatbot design to adults who befriend children to extract their secrets. The most striking remedy sought is a proportional share of OpenAI itself, built on the analogy that children's data are the grapes and the models are the wine. She then turns to schools, recalling an FTC amicus brief warning that schools can no longer consent on behalf of parents to data collection by EdTech products. Citing Internet Safety Labs, she notes that 96 percent of such products collect data on children without consent. Her argument is that EdTech is Big Tech in a sweater vest and that schools will have to face parental consent as parents wake up.
points: The lawsuit centers on consent, claiming that children cannot legally consent to the use of their data and that OpenAI collected it without parental permission.
Cherkin compares chatbot design that invites children to share secrets with grooming behavior that no adult could lawfully carry out in person.
The requested remedy of a proportional share of the company rests on the logic that children's data are inseparable from the trained models.
An FTC amicus brief means schools can no longer stand in for parents when consenting to data collection by EdTech products.
Schools sign off on products from huge companies without informing parents, a practice that parental awareness is likely to end.
quotes: The complaint alleges that OpenAI takes data from children without parental consent and that in doing so, they violate several existing laws, enrich their own coffers, and harm children in the process.
No adult is allowed to do this to a child in person. OpenAI’s position is that it’s fine as long as a computer does it.
Of course, it should go without saying, but children are not small adults, and their brains are not fully developed.
In other words, children’s data are the grapes; OpenAI’s models are the wine.
This amicus brief establishes that schools can no longer stand in the shoes of parents for the purpose of consenting to data collection.
Internet Safety Labs has found that 96% of these products collect data about children without consent.
In education, schools sign off on permitting multi-million and billion dollar companies to collect information about children without informing parents.
